newsitem.title: USA: Rural New York hideaway to host Cypriot leaders.
newsitem.headline: Rural New York hideaway to host Cypriot leaders.

text.p: The leaders of the Greek and Turkish Cypriots will meet next month at a beautiful, historical inn and conference centre called Troutbeck, 90 miles (145 kms) north of New York city.

According to present plans, Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides, as head of the Greek Cypriot community, and Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash will hold intensive talks from July 9 to 13 to try to revive long-dormant negotiations aimed at reuniting their divided island.

Troutbeck comprises a 442 acre (180 hectares) estate, about half the size of New York's Central Park. According to the center's own advertising material, it was a "gathering place for literati and liberals" during the 1920s.
Nowadays, it offers "wondrous weddings," "wonderful weekends" and a "brilliant kitchen."
Clerides and Denktash are more likely to be using the facilities offered for business conferences.
"It's exclusive, it's delicious, but you came here to work," one of the center's own web pages gently reminds guests who arrive without thoughts of matrimony or a fun weekend.
"Our dazzling new Great Room/Corporate Centre has the room you need for expansive thinking ... The net net is that you accomplish more at Troutbeck."
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan very much hopes so.

He will preside over an opening ceremony and then leave matters in the hands of his special adviser for Cyprus, former Ecuadorean Foreign Minister Diego Cordovez, who has 25 years' experience as a senior U.N. official and helped negotiate a settlement for Afghanistan.
"When the official work day is over, instead of all the diversions of a metropolitan centre, you'll find yourselves still dealing with each other, but on a different level," says the brochure.
Again, the United Nations hopes so. It has been trying for decades to bring Greek and Turkish Cypriots back together under a bi-zonal, bi-communal government.

Cyprus has been virtually partitioned since 1974 when troops from Turkey took over the north of the island after a coup in Nicosia engineered by the junta then ruling Greece. But the two communities have been estranged since 1963, when a government comprising representatives of both fell apart little more than three years after independence from Britain.
A major attraction of Troutbeck is what it calls its "brilliant kitchen" -- a claim borne out by visitors.

Should the conferees complete their work with unusual haste, they will have at their disposal a 12,000 book library, videotaped movies, tennis courts, swimming pools and an 18-hole golf course in a nearby town.
And how much will all this cost?

Neither the United Nations nor Corcoran is saying. But, according to the center's brochure, two nights for two people enjoying one of Troutbeck's "wonderful weekends" runs from $650 to $1,050 -- six meals and open bar included.
